stem: A bank's compliance pipeline classifies 10,000 transaction alerts per day into risk tiers under a 2-second latency budget, and drafts the referral letter language sent to a named regulator whenever a tier triggers escalation. Which model strategy should be used?

opts.t: Use the smallest, fastest model for every step, since the volume and latency budget dominate the task.
Route bulk classification to the fast model, but reserve a higher-capability model for drafting the regulator referral text.
Run the entire pipeline, including bulk classification, on the highest-capability model available, to be safe.
Fine-tune the fast model on past referral letters instead of testing whether a stronger base model suffices.

whyRight: The volume and latency budget fit the fast model for bulk classification, but the referral text requires open-ended judgment when addressing a regulator — a rung the fast model's own accuracy bar wasn't built to clear, so that step alone needs the higher-capability model.

whyWrong.A: Volume and latency alone would justify this for pure classification, but the stem's own escalation requirement is an open-ended judgment call this model can't reliably clear.
whyWrong.C: Upgrading bulk classification too adds cost and latency the 2-second budget doesn't have room for, when only the escalation step needs the extra capability.
whyWrong.D: Fine-tuning is the expensive lever; it doesn't test whether a stronger base model already handles regulator-facing drafting without any additional training.

t1Clause: drafts the referral letter language sent to a named regulator whenever a tier triggers escalation
lessonKey: bulk but capability classification drafting fast higher model referral regulator reserve route text

stem: A subscription service's support-agent system prompt refuses any discussion of account cancellation, correctly blocking retention-abuse requests. A consumer-protection rule now requires the same agent to process cancellations within 48 hours when requested through a dedicated retention tool, with legal sign-off. What should change?

opts.t: Add the exception into the system prompt's top-level guardrail language, so it applies to every tool.
Add a scoped exception to the retention tool's own system prompt, leaving the blanket guardrail in place elsewhere.
Move the cancellation check into client-side validation before requests ever reach the model.
Document the new exception in team onboarding materials, without changing the system prompt itself.

whyRight: The blanket guardrail still correctly blocks retention abuse elsewhere, so it should stay; the legitimate need is scoped to one tool, and guardrails belong at the layer where the exception actually applies — a per-tool addition, not a blanket rewrite.

whyWrong.A: The need is scoped to one tool; rewriting the top-level guardrail applies the exception everywhere, undoing protection the guardrail still correctly provides elsewhere.
whyWrong.C: A client-side check never reaches the model itself — the same failure as setting a behavioral rule through an environment variable.
whyWrong.D: Documentation elsewhere in the pipeline never reaches the model as an instruction, so its behavior toward cancellation requests won't change.

t1Clause: when requested through a dedicated retention tool
lessonKey: add blanket elsewhere exception guardrail leaving own place prompt retention s scoped system tool

stem: A multi-step reconciliation agent compares entries across 12 ledgers using a step-by-step reasoning cue; a prior test without the cue produced a higher error rate. A product manager proposes dropping the cue now, since responses already return within budget. What should happen?

opts.t: Keep the reasoning cue; the prior test already showed accuracy drops on this task without it.
Drop the cue now that latency is within budget, since token savings outweigh a one-time test result.
Replace the reasoning cue with a bounded scratchpad to cut tokens while preserving most of the accuracy benefit.
Remove the cue, since the task's format looks similar to previous single-step tasks that didn't need one.

whyRight: The task is genuinely multi-step, and the cue is already verified necessary: removing it earlier measurably raised the error rate. Nothing in the stem states a latency conflict, so the sophisticated-sounding token-saving proposal would reopen the accuracy failure the cue was added to prevent.

whyWrong.B: The prior test already measured a higher error rate without the cue; token savings don't outweigh evidence the stem itself provides.
whyWrong.C: This targets a latency conflict the stem never states exists; the plain cue already works without needing to be bounded.
whyWrong.D: The task compares entries across 12 ledgers in multiple steps; treating it as single-step misreads its actual shape.

t1Clause: since responses already return within budget
lessonKey: accuracy already cue drops keep prior reasoning showed task test without

stem: An HR assistant answers thousands of daily employee queries from a 40-page benefits handbook containing about 30 scattered bullet facts, none more critical than another, and keeps missing facts buried in the middle of the document. What should be changed?

opts.t: Leave the document's structure unchanged, since it's well under the model's effective context window.
Pull the single most business-critical fact into a highlighted block near the top of the handbook.
Convert the scattered bullets into explicit headed sections grouped by topic, even without one dominant fact.
Shorten the handbook to a strict length limit before employee queries reach the model.

whyRight: No single fact in the handbook is more critical than another, so the fix is structural, not a top-of-document highlight built for one dominant fact. Headed sections grouped by topic restore retrievability across the whole middle, which a 40-page scattered-bullet document actually needs.

whyWrong.A: A 40-page handbook queried thousands of times a day is exactly the scale the effect occurs at; 'short input' doesn't describe this document.
whyWrong.B: The stem states no fact is more critical than another, so highlighting a single fact targets a problem this handbook doesn't have.
whyWrong.D: Shortening under a length limit risks cutting exactly the scattered facts that are already going missing.

lessonKey: convert even explicit findings first grouped headed one sections summary topic without

stem: A legal team requires a compliance disclaimer that reflects today's date to appear first in a high-volume, latency-sensitive support prompt built on a large, byte-identical cached prefix. Which placement satisfies the compliance requirement without invalidating the cache?

opts.t: Insert the disclaimer ahead of the cached prefix, as the literal first bytes of the prompt.
Keep the prefix ordering unchanged, adding the disclaimer as the next block after it.
Split the static prefix around the disclaimer so it sits mid-block, preserving partial reuse of the surrounding text.
Disable caching for this prompt and regenerate the full prefix with the disclaimer prepended on every call.

whyRight: The compliance requirement is about the disclaimer's presence and prominence, not its literal byte position. Keeping the static prefix first and adding the disclaimer immediately after it preserves the byte-identical cache while still surfacing the disclaimer at the very start of the response.

whyWrong.A: Treats 'first' as a literal byte-position requirement rather than the compliance team's actual intent, and inserting dynamic content ahead of the prefix invalidates the entire cache.
whyWrong.C: Splitting the prefix around the disclaimer breaks the single stable prefix caching depends on, so the surrounding text is no longer byte-identical across calls.
whyWrong.D: Discards a working cost and latency lever the workload doesn't need to give up, when the compliance need is satisfiable without disabling caching at all.

t1Clause: the prompt is called at high volume, so the cached prefix stays within the cache's retention window
lessonKey: adding after block disclaimer keep next ordering prefix unchanged

stem: A contract-review pipeline runs 200 calls a day on a mid-tier model. One step needs deep reasoning over ambiguous, high-stakes clauses, and latency isn't a stated limit there. What is the lowest-cost change that meets the requirement without over-provisioning the rest of the pipeline?

opts.t: Enable extended thinking only for the ambiguous-clause step, leaving the rest of the pipeline on the current model.
Move the entire pipeline to a larger, more capable model to raise reasoning quality everywhere.
Add a strict token budget to the ambiguous step to control cost, without changing how it reasons.
Fine-tune the current model on past contract decisions before touching this step's reasoning approach.

whyRight: Extended thinking is the lightest lever that reaches the reasoning depth the ambiguous step needs, leaving the other 200 daily calls on their current, cheaper model. Upgrading the entire pipeline reaches for a far more expensive rung the stated requirement never calls for.

whyWrong.B: Upgrading the entire pipeline raises capability everywhere the requirement doesn't call for it, adding cost and latency to 200 daily calls to fix a bottleneck in one step.
whyWrong.C: A token budget controls spend but does nothing for reasoning quality on an ambiguous, high-stakes step — the bottleneck is depth, not tokens.
whyWrong.D: Fine-tuning requires curating training data and a retraining cycle before it touches this step's reasoning, an expensive detour around a same-day fix.

t1Clause: the reasoning gap is isolated to one step in the pipeline rather than spread across most of the workload
lessonKey: enable extended larger model moving rather step than thinking whole workload

stem: A support bot's tool-routing prompt has six few-shot examples, all drawn from the most common, easily-routed requests, yet still misroutes high-value escalation requests weekly, flagged by the support-ops lead. Applying the principle that examples must target the failure distribution, which change is correct?

opts.t: Add three or four examples demonstrating the exact required response format for escalation replies.
Add a post-processing classifier that flags likely misroutes for a human reviewer to catch after the fact.
Keep the six examples as they are and add a default-tool fallback for any ambiguous escalation request.
Replace the six examples with new ones drawn from the actual misrouted escalation cases.

whyRight: Few-shot examples teach by pattern-matching to what they show; examples drawn from easy, common cases don't resemble the ambiguous escalation requests actually failing. Replacing them with examples from the observed failure distribution targets exactly the pattern the prompt is missing, regardless of how many examples existed before.

whyWrong.A: This targets output-formatting precision, a real fix for inconsistent formatting, but the stated failure is misrouting to the wrong tool, not inconsistent response format.
whyWrong.B: A classifier that flags likely misroutes for a human catches failures after they happen instead of fixing the routing prompt itself.
whyWrong.C: A generic fallback for ambiguous requests contradicts the stated fact that these are high-value escalations needing correct, specific routing.

t1Clause: the bot misroutes ambiguous escalation requests to the wrong tool
lessonKey: distribution drawn examples failure observed replace them

stem: A coding-assistant session runs hundreds of turns. An early instruction — never modify files under one protected directory — must hold for the rest of the session, while older turns are summarized to control token cost. Which design satisfies both?

opts.t: Let the rule live inside the rolling summary along with everything else from early turns.
Pin the never-modify-this-directory rule in a persistent structured block, re-included every call, kept separate from the rolling summary.
Stop summarizing altogether and resend the full unabridged history every call to guarantee nothing is lost.
Move the protected-directory rule into the system prompt once, then drop it from every later call to save tokens.

whyRight: Pinning the rule into a stable structured block that sits outside the rolling summary guarantees it is resent unchanged every call, while the rest of the conversation still gets summarized to control token growth. A rule that must never change needs a slot summarization never touches.

whyWrong.A: Repeated re-summarization passes can paraphrase or drop the rule over hundreds of turns, risking exactly the drift a never-change requirement cannot tolerate.
whyWrong.C: Resending the full unabridged history defeats the stated goal of controlling token cost as the conversation grows, an unneeded trade for a single pinned fact.
whyWrong.D: Dropping the rule from later calls assumes the API remembers it between requests, but nothing sent in an earlier call persists unless it is resent.

t1Clause: the early decision must hold unchanged for the rest of the session
lessonKey: block call decision every included into persistent pin re rolling separate structured summary
